meta.blurb: At Maple Court, four retired friends meet every Wednesday over cake to solve old crimes. When the owner who wanted to sell their beloved garden is found dead in the glasshouse, they get a real mystery, with a locked door and a lie about a train.
meta.bible: Edith Marsh: retired headteacher, sharp and calm, keeps a notebook in her cardigan pocket. Walter Pike: retired railway signalman who knows every timetable. Meera Shah: retired nurse. Fergus Lyle: retired locksmith, gnarled hands, loves a good lock. Together they are the Wednesday Club and meet at three o'clock in the Garden Room with tea and lemon cake. Conrad Vane: the new owner of Maple Court, sharp suit, cold at first, secretly changes his mind and writes a letter on Saturday withdrawing the sale. Harold Stott: Vane's finance manager, round and rosy, polished black shoes, steals money from residents' care fees; the killer. Joe Bell: the gardener for twenty years, gruff and honest; Saturday night at his daughter's house. Lucy Pym: the young cook. Gwen Hartley: eighty-eight, planted all the roses, uses a walking stick, saw a man in a long raincoat at nine. Sergeant Tom Rudd: tall young police officer. Ruth Vane: Conrad's sister, who inherits Maple Court. Maple Court: a brick house turned into flats for older people. Willowby: the small town. Glasshouse: at the end of the garden, full of tomatoes and seedlings; the door locks only from outside with a key; three keys exist: Vane's, Joe's and a spare in the office cabinet with a four-figure code known to Joe, Lucy and Stott. Facts: the pots are bright red clay; on Saturday there was no railway service because of track repairs, only replacement buses, so Stott's six-fifteen train did not exist; Stott signed out of the visitors' book at six; Vane was struck at the back of the head; Vane's letter was hidden in a seed tin; the secret that the pots were pulled down on top of him was told only to Edith. Voice and tone: warm, gently funny and clear, a fair-play puzzle for older readers; the death is stated plainly with no gore; Stott confesses and is arrested.

beats.scene: A sunny old house with a long garden and a glass greenhouse behind it
beats.summary: Maple Court is a friendly old house in the town of Willowby, turned into homes for older people, with a lovely garden and a Glasshouse.

beats.scene: Four friends around a table with tea, cake and a newspaper puzzle
beats.summary: Four friends meet every Wednesday in the Garden Room to drink tea and solve puzzles from old newspapers.

beats.summary: Gwen Hartley, who is eighty-eight, protests that she planted every rose in the garden.

beats.scene: Gwen Hartley carries a tray of seedlings past a lit glasshouse at dusk
beats.summary: At nine o'clock Gwen goes to fetch her seedlings and sees a light in the Glasshouse and a man in a long raincoat.

beats.scene: Edith speaks quietly to Sergeant Rudd on the front steps of Maple Court
beats.summary: Edith persuades Sergeant Rudd to keep the case open, and he privately tells her about the smashed pots but asks her to keep it secret.

beats.scene: Joe sits with a mug in a potting shed, frowning at his boots

beats.scene: Gwen Hartley in a floral chair, pointing out to the glasshouse window
beats.summary: Gwen tells the friends about the light and the man in the long raincoat, whose face she could not see.

beats.scene: Lucy Pym, the young cook, holds a tray with an untouched dinner
beats.summary: Lucy Pym the cook says Mr Vane told her he had a meeting at nine o'clock in the Glasshouse.

beats.scene: A visitors' book lies open on a desk, a finger on the last name
beats.summary: The visitors' book shows that only Harold Stott signed out on Saturday evening, at six o'clock.

beats.scene: Harold Stott sits in the manager's office with a polite, sad expression
beats.summary: Stott tells the friends he left for London at six, caught the train and heard the news only on Monday.

beats.scene: Fergus and Walter examine a scratched lock and red clay shards
beats.summary: The sergeant lets the club into the Glasshouse, where Fergus finds scratches on the lock and Walter notices red clay pots.

beats.summary: Edith finds a letter in a seed tin: Mr Vane has decided on Saturday not to sell the garden after all.

beats.scene: Meera sits beside Gwen Hartley holding a bank statement under a lamp
beats.summary: Meera sees on Gwen's care-fee statement that she has been charged twice each month.

beats.scene: Meera and Fergus go from door to door with a notebook in the corridor
beats.summary: Several other residents have also been charged the same hidden fee every month.

beats.summary: Edith notices that Stott's polished shoes have red dust on them, though he says he has not been near the garden.

beats.summary: Walter checks the station notice: there were no trains at all on Saturday, only replacement buses.

beats.summary: Fergus finds red clay dust on the tag of the spare Glasshouse key in the office cabinet.

beats.summary: Lucy says that only Stott, Joe and she knew the cabinet's code, and that she did not take the key.

beats.summary: Sergeant Rudd says that lies and red dust are not proof, and he needs Stott to say something only the killer would know.

beats.summary: Edith plans a trap: a residents' meeting where she will tell the news carefully and wait for Stott to slip.

beats.summary: The friends rehearse: Walter will mention the train, Meera the extra fees, and Fergus the red-stained key.

beats.summary: Stott tells the meeting that the sale of the garden must go ahead, and the residents groan.

beats.scene: Edith stands with her notebook in front of a quiet room
beats.summary: Edith stands and tells the meeting simply that Mr Vane was found dead in the Glasshouse after a fall.

beats.scene: Harold Stott frowns with his mouth open, a flowerpot on the table behind him
beats.summary: Stott slips: he sighs about poor Mr Vane lying under all those pots that someone pulled down.

beats.scene: Edith points a finger calmly at Harold Stott across the chairs
beats.summary: Edith asks Stott how he knows that the pots were pulled down on Mr Vane when nobody has been told.

beats.scene: Joe stands at the back of the lounge, arms folded, shaking his head
beats.summary: Stott says Joe told him, but Joe says from the back of the room that he told no one.

beats.scene: Walter holds up a yellow railway notice as the residents murmur
beats.summary: Walter and Meera put the lies and the extra fees to Stott: no train ran on Saturday, and the care fees were doubled.

beats.summary: Joe keeps his job, and Gwen plants a rose bush in memory of Conrad Vane.

B1B2: Maple Court is an old house in the town of Willowby, now divided into homes for older people. Its greatest treasure is a long garden, with a rose walk, a vegetable patch and a glasshouse at the end.
Every Wednesday afternoon, four friends meet in the Garden Room with tea and cake. They call themselves the Wednesday Club, and they spend the time solving old crimes from the newspapers for fun.
Edith Marsh was a headteacher, and she can tell when anyone is lying. Walter Pike worked on the railway, Meera Shah was a nurse, and Fergus Lyle opened and mended locks for fifty years.
A new owner, Mr Conrad Vane, arrives in a sharp suit and pins a notice to the board in the hall. It says that the garden will be sold to builders at the end of the summer.
Gwen Hartley, who is eighty-eight, stands beside her rose bushes and says that she planted every one of them. She tells Mr Vane that he would have to dig her up first.
Joe Bell, the gardener, has looked after Maple Court for twenty years. When he learns that he will lose his job along with the garden, he shouts at Mr Vane in front of everyone.
On Friday afternoon Mr Vane tells the residents in the lounge that the decision is final. Beside him stands his finance manager, Harold Stott, who smiles in a friendly way and says nothing.

On Saturday the residents hold a summer fair on the lawn, with cakes, flags and a raffle. Walter grumbles that the railway line is closed all weekend for work on the track, so buses are running instead.
At six o'clock Harold Stott signs out in the visitors' book at the front desk. He tells the receptionist, cheerfully, that he is going to catch the evening train to London.
At nine o'clock that night, Gwen goes down the garden to bring in her seedlings. She sees a light shining in the glasshouse and a man in a long raincoat inside, but she cannot see his face.
On Sunday morning Joe finds the glasshouse door locked. He opens it with his key and finds Mr Vane lying on the floor, among broken flowerpots, and he runs to call for help.
Sergeant Tom Rudd and the doctor examine the glasshouse and decide it was an accident. They say that Mr Vane must have slipped on the wet floor and hit his head, and that is that.
That evening the four friends meet in the Garden Room, and for once nobody eats the cake. Edith says that she does not believe it was an accident, and her friends lean in to listen.
Fergus explains that the glasshouse lock needs a key, and it can only be turned from outside. So if Mr Vane was alone and fell, then someone else must have locked the door afterwards.
Fergus counts the keys that fit the glasshouse door. Mr Vane had one, Joe has another, and a spare hangs in the office cabinet, which opens with a four-number code.
Meera, who was allowed to see Mr Vane, says that the mark was on the back of his head. She is a nurse, and she says that it looks like a blow, not a fall.

Edith speaks to Sergeant Rudd on the steps, and he agrees to keep the case open for a few days. He tells her something in secret about the smashed flowerpots, and asks her to tell no one outside the club.
Joe admits that he shouted at Mr Vane, but says he was at his daughter's house all Saturday night. His daughter has already told the sergeant that this is true.
Gwen tells the friends about the light in the glasshouse and the man she saw there. He was tall and wore a long raincoat, but she cannot say if it was Mr Vane or somebody else.
Lucy Pym, the young cook, says that she took a dinner tray to Mr Vane's office on Saturday. He did not eat it, and he told her that he had a meeting at nine o'clock in the glasshouse.
Edith studies the visitors' book and finds that only one person left after the fair. It was Harold Stott, who signed out at six o'clock, which fits exactly with what he said.
Harold Stott, in the manager's office, tells the friends that he left at six and took the train to London. He says that he only learned of Mr Vane's death on Monday morning, and he looks very sad.
The sergeant lets the club into the glasshouse for ten minutes. Fergus finds fresh scratches around the keyhole, and Walter notices that the broken pots are made of a bright red clay.
Edith opens a small seed tin on the potting bench and finds a folded letter inside. It is signed by Mr Vane and dated Saturday, and it says that he has decided not to sell the garden.

On Monday Harold Stott announces that the garden sale will go ahead as planned, in spite of Mr Vane's death. Edith wonders who knew that Mr Vane had changed his mind, and who would lose if the garden were saved.
Meera visits Gwen and reads her monthly bill for the care she receives. She sees that the same fee has been charged twice every month, once as a care fee and once as an office fee.
Meera and Fergus knock at the doors along the corridor and ask politely to see some bills. Many other residents have been charged the same strange fee every month, and none of them noticed.
On Monday morning Edith notices something about Harold Stott's polished shoes. They are covered with a fine red dust, and he told the club that he has not been anywhere near the garden.

Walter walks to the station to check something that has been bothering him. A large notice confirms that no trains ran on Saturday, because the line was closed and buses took everyone to the next town.
Walter finds the replacement bus driver and shows him a photograph of Harold Stott. The driver says that the first evening bus left at twenty to seven, and he is sure he did not see this man.
Fergus opens the office cabinet with the help of Lucy, and he takes out the spare glasshouse key. On its tag he finds a smear of the same bright red clay that was on Stott's shoes.
Lucy tells Fergus that only three people know the code to the key cabinet. They are Joe, herself and Harold Stott, and she says that she did not use it on Saturday and neither did Joe.
The friends tell Sergeant Rudd everything, and he agrees that it looks bad for Stott. However, lies and red dust are not proof, and he needs Stott to say something that only the killer could know.
Edith has an idea and draws a plan in her notebook. She will call a meeting of all the residents, tell everyone about Mr Vane's death carefully and wait for Harold Stott to make a mistake.
The friends practise in the Garden Room until they are ready. Walter will speak about the missing train, Meera about the strange fees, and Fergus will show the key with red dust on it.
On Thursday morning the lounge is full of residents sitting on rows of chairs. Harold Stott stands at the front with a friendly smile, and the sergeant waits quietly in the next room.
Stott speaks first and says that, sadly, the sale of the garden must go ahead. He says that the company needs the money, and the residents groan and shake their heads.
Edith stands and asks everyone to remember Mr Vane. She says only that he was found in the glasshouse on Sunday morning after a fall, and that it seemed to be a sad accident.
Stott shakes his head and sighs, and then he says something he should not. He says that it is dreadful to think of poor Conrad lying under all those pots that somebody pulled down on top of him.
Edith asks quietly how Mr Stott knew about the pots, since nobody outside the police has been told. Only three people, she says, have ever heard such a thing.
Stott says quickly that Joe must have told him about the pots. Joe stands up at the back of the room, arms folded, and says clearly that he has not said one word to anybody.
Now Walter stands up and holds up the yellow railway notice. He says that no trains ran on Saturday, and Meera adds that Stott has been charging residents a fee that nobody understands.
Fergus stands and holds up the spare glasshouse key, with its tag stained red. He says that only three people knew the cabinet code, and the clay on the key matches the dust on Stott's shoes.
Harold Stott falls into a chair and covers his face. He confesses that Mr Vane found the stolen money, and that in a panic he struck him with a pot.
Sergeant Rudd steps in through the half-open door and takes Harold Stott by the arm. He says calmly that he is arresting him for the death of Conrad Vane and for stealing the residents' money.
In the following weeks the police recover most of the stolen money from Stott's bank accounts. A lawyer arranges for every resident to be paid back, and Gwen Hartley receives hers first.
Mr Vane's sister, Ruth, inherits Maple Court and reads the letter that Edith found in the seed tin. She signs a paper that says the garden will never be sold, as her brother wished on his last day.
Joe keeps his job, and the garden is safe. On a bright morning Gwen Hartley plants a new rose bush in memory of Conrad Vane, with Joe digging the hole.

On the next Wednesday, Sergeant Rudd arrives at the Garden Room door with a box of cakes and a thick folder. He says that the police could use some advice, and he asks if the club could help with a puzzle.

In the evening light the four friends sit in the garden with their tea, and the glasshouse glows behind them like a lantern. The roses are blooming, the house is quiet, and the next puzzle is waiting.
C1C2: Maple Court stood at the edge of the little town of Willowby, a tall brick house that had been divided into comfortable flats for people who had finished with work and not yet finished with life. Behind it lay a long garden, with a rose walk, a vegetable patch and, at the far end, a glasshouse full of tomatoes and seedlings. Every resident had a favourite corner of it, and none of them imagined that it could ever be taken away.

Every Wednesday at three o'clock, four friends settled into the Garden Room with a pot of strong tea and a large lemon cake. They called themselves the Wednesday Club, and their favourite pastime was to lay out an old crime from the newspaper cuttings and argue cheerfully about who had done it. None of them had ever solved a real case, but they had often guessed the answer before the last page.

Edith Marsh, who had been a headteacher for thirty years, could still detect a fib at twenty paces and kept her notebook in her cardigan pocket. Walter Pike had spent his working life in a railway signal box and knew every timetable in the county by heart. Meera Shah had nursed the sick for four decades, and Fergus Lyle had picked, mended and made locks for fifty years, so that together they formed a most unusual company of detectives.

In the spring Maple Court was bought by a company, and its new owner, Mr Conrad Vane, swept into the hall in a sharp suit and pinned a notice to the board. It announced, in brisk, businesslike sentences, that the garden would be sold to builders at the end of the summer, to pay for the modernising of the house. A silence fell over the residents who read it, and then a great many people began to speak at once.

Eighty-eight-year-old Gwen Hartley stood among her roses with her walking stick planted firmly in the grass and declared that she had set every single bush in the ground with her own hands. If the new owner wished to sell the garden, she told him, with a spark in her pale eyes, he would have to dig her up first. Mr Vane smiled thinly and said that he had no wish to dig anybody up, but that business was business.

Joe Bell had cared for the gardens of Maple Court for twenty years, and when he discovered that the sale would cost him his job as well as his beloved vegetables, he lost his temper. Standing beside a wheelbarrow of weeds, he shouted at Mr Vane so loudly that the pigeons flew up from the lawn, and half the residents heard every word. Mr Vane only turned and walked back toward the house, though his neck had turned a dull red.

On Friday afternoon the residents gathered in the lounge, and Mr Vane informed them coldly that his decision was final and that no petition would change it. At his side stood his finance manager, Harold Stott, a round, rosy man with a briefcase, who smiled warmly at everyone and shook his head as though the whole matter were a great pity. Edith, who had seen many pupils lie, observed that the smile never reached his eyes.

On Saturday the residents held their summer fair on the lawn, with cakes, flags, a tombola and a brass band of very old gentlemen. Walter Pike, who read railway notices as other people read novels, grumbled to everyone within earshot that the line was closed for the whole weekend for work on the track, and that buses were running in place of trains. Nobody paid the smallest attention, since nobody at Maple Court was planning to travel.

At six o'clock, when the stalls were being folded away, Harold Stott signed the visitors' book at the front desk with a flourish. He announced to everyone who would listen that he was off to catch the quarter-past-six train to London, where he had business, and that he would not be back until Monday morning. The receptionist waved him off cheerfully, and he strolled out of the front door swinging his briefcase.

At nine o'clock that evening, Gwen Hartley crept down the garden in her slippers to rescue her seedlings from the damp night air. A light was burning in the glasshouse, and through the misted glass she glimpsed a tall figure in a long raincoat standing very still beside the benches. She turned back at once, not wishing to intrude, and told herself that it was only Mr Vane inspecting his tomatoes.

On Sunday morning Joe Bell arrived early to water the tomatoes and found the glasshouse door locked, which struck him as odd, since he had left it unlocked the evening before. He turned his key and stepped inside, and there, among a heap of smashed flowerpots, lay Mr Conrad Vane, quite still. Joe backed out of the door with his heart thumping and ran for the house to call for help.

Sergeant Tom Rudd, a tall young man with a worried frown, arrived within the hour with the doctor, and between them they examined the scene for ten minutes. The conclusion seemed obvious to both: Mr Vane had slipped on the wet floor, knocked over a shelf of pots and struck his head as he fell. A tragic accident, the sergeant said with a sigh, and he began to close his notebook as though the whole matter were already settled.

That evening the Wednesday Club gathered in the Garden Room, and for the first time anyone could remember, the lemon cake sat untouched in the middle of the table. Edith Marsh announced that she did not believe for one moment that Conrad Vane's death had been an accident, and that something in the story had been nagging at her all day. Her three friends, who had trusted her judgement for years, leaned forward to hear why.

The door was the first thing that troubled her, Edith said, and Fergus, who had spent half a century with locks, nodded gravely. That particular lock, he explained, could be turned only with a key from the outside, so a man who fell alone inside it could not possibly have locked himself in. Someone, he concluded, must have stood on the path, turned the key and walked away, leaving Mr Vane where he lay.

Fergus counted on his gnarled fingers the keys that fitted the glasshouse door, and there were only three in the whole of Maple Court. One had been found in Mr Vane's pocket and a second belonged to Joe, while the third hung in the office cabinet, a steel box that opened with a four-figure code. Whoever had locked that door, Fergus said gravely, had used one of the three, and the owner of the third was a mystery.

The sergeant had allowed Meera, as a retired nurse, to look at Mr Vane before the ambulance came, and she now described what she had noticed with calm, professional care. The mark lay at the back of his head, she explained, and it was the wrong shape and in the wrong place for a man who had pitched forward onto a shelf of clay pots. Everything about it, she said, suggested a single hard blow from behind or from the side.

Edith cornered the sergeant on the front steps, and though he began by protesting, she presented her friends' observations so crisply that he finally agreed to keep the case open a few days. He added, in a low voice, that one detail had not been told to anyone: the heap of smashed flowerpots had been deliberately pulled down on top of Mr Vane after he fell. It was a secret, he said, and she must promise not to repeat it outside her four friends.

Joe Bell was gruff but honest when they found him in the potting shed, and he admitted at once that he had shouted at Mr Vane and meant every word. He would never have harmed the man, he said, and on Saturday night he had been at his daughter's house across town, eating roast chicken and watching the television. The sergeant had already checked with his daughter, who had confirmed it, and the friends crossed him off their list.

Gwen Hartley, wrapped in a shawl in her favourite chair, told the friends everything she had seen at nine o'clock on Saturday night, and her voice trembled slightly as she did so. There had been a light, she said, and a tall man in a long raincoat standing absolutely motionless, but because of the mist on the glass she could not be sure that he was Mr Vane. She had gone back to bed, she added with a small, ashamed shake of her head, and had never thought to tell anyone.

Lucy Pym, the young cook, was almost in tears when Meera found her in the kitchen, for she had carried a dinner tray up to Mr Vane's office on Saturday evening and brought it down again untouched. He had been in a very odd mood, she remembered, and had told her that he had an important meeting at nine o'clock in the glasshouse, where nobody would overhear. She had not thought to ask with whom, and now she wished more than anything that she had.

Edith asked the receptionist to show her the visitors' book for Saturday, and she ran her eye down the names with a headteacher's thorough attention. Almost every visitor had left by five, and the only person to sign out after the fair had closed was Harold Stott, who had written the time carefully as six o'clock. It fitted exactly with his own account, and for the moment, at least, it was impossible to say anything against him.

Harold Stott received the club in the manager's office with an air of weary sadness, pouring them each a glass of water he did not seem to notice they had refused. He had left at six o'clock, he said, caught the quarter-past-six train to London and spent the evening with his sister, and he had learned of poor Conrad's death only on Monday morning. His story was clear, his manner correct, and Edith could not find a single seam in it.

The sergeant, who was beginning to like his new advisers, let the club into the glasshouse for ten minutes under his watchful eye. Fergus knelt at the door and found fresh scratches around the keyhole, as if the key had been turned in a hurry, while Walter noticed that the shattered pots were of a bright red clay that stained everything. Such details, Edith murmured, were not what an honest accident bothered to leave behind.

Behind a row of seed packets, Edith noticed a small tin that was heavier than seed should have been, and inside it she found a letter folded in four. It was signed by Conrad Vane and dated that very Saturday, and in firm, plain words it withdrew his plan to sell the garden, for reasons he promised to explain on Monday. The man the whole of Maple Court had hated, Edith realised with a shock, had changed his mind on the last day of his life.

By Monday morning Harold Stott had pinned a new notice to the board in the hall, declaring that the sale of the garden would proceed exactly as planned in spite of poor Mr Vane's death. Edith read it twice, and a thought began to form in her mind like a pencil sketch becoming a drawing. Who had known that Conrad Vane had changed his mind, she asked her friends, and who stood to lose most if the garden were saved?

Gwen asked Meera, as a trusted former nurse, to look at the monthly statement for her care fees, because the figures had always confused her. Meera read the page twice and then a third time, and discovered that the same sum had been charged each month under two slightly different names. One was a care fee, and the other an administration fee that did not seem to belong to any rule, and it had been going on, according to the dates, for more than two years.

Meera and Fergus went quietly from door to door along the corridors, asking the residents, as casually as they could, whether they would mind showing them their latest statements. At least fourteen of the people they spoke to had been paying the same unexplained administration fee, month after month, and not one of them had thought to question it. Together the sums were large, and somebody, Meera said grimly, had been pocketing them.

On Monday morning Edith noticed that Harold Stott's black shoes, which were normally polished to the brilliance of mirrors, were dusted around the welts with a fine, brick-red powder. He had told the club that he had not stepped into the garden since the fair, and the colour of the dust matched, to a shade, the clay of the broken pots in the glasshouse. She said nothing, but her pencil moved busily across the page of her notebook.

Something had been tugging at Walter's mind ever since Harold Stott's story, and he walked down to Willowby station on Tuesday morning to settle the matter. The large yellow notice pinned beside the ticket office confirmed what he had grumbled about at the summer fair: there had been no trains on Saturday, none at all, because the line had been closed for track repairs. The quarter-past-six train to London, therefore, had never existed outside the imagination of Harold Stott.

Walter tracked down the driver of the Saturday evening replacement bus, who was drinking tea in the depot, and showed him a small photograph of Harold Stott from the Maple Court newsletter. The man studied it carefully, then shook his head, saying that the first bus had left at twenty to seven with six passengers and that a round, rosy gentleman with a briefcase was certainly not among them. So Stott had not caught his train, and he had not caught the bus either.

With Lucy's help Fergus opened the steel cabinet in the office and lifted down the spare key to the glasshouse, turning it carefully in the light from the window. On the paper tag attached to it, and on the teeth, he found a faint smear of that same brick-red clay, which was precisely the colour of the shattered pots and of the dust on Harold Stott's shoes. It was the first piece of physical evidence they had found, and it pointed in exactly one direction.

Lucy explained, with a nervous glance toward the door, that only three people in the whole building knew the four-figure code that opened the key cabinet: Joe, herself and Harold Stott. She had not touched the spare key on Saturday, she said, and Joe had been miles away at his daughter's, which left exactly one candidate. Fergus, who had always trusted a good lock to tell the truth, thanked her and made a note.

The friends laid everything before Sergeant Rudd in the Garden Room, point by point, like lawyers presenting a case, and he listened to every word with his pen tapping his notebook. It looked very bad for Harold Stott, he conceded, but a false story about a train and a little red dust would not satisfy a court, and he needed something more. What would convince a jury, he said, was Stott saying something that only the person who had been in the glasshouse could possibly know.

Edith, who had spent thirty years extracting confessions from guilty schoolboys, drew a plan in her notebook with the neatness of a general before a battle. She would call a meeting of every resident, give the news of Mr Vane's death in the simplest possible words, and then let Harold Stott, who loved the sound of his own voice, talk until he said too much. Sergeant Rudd would wait in the next room, and the others would sit quietly among the residents.

That afternoon the Wednesday Club rehearsed in the Garden Room like a small theatre company, with Walter clutching a copy of the railway notice, Meera holding a handful of statements and Fergus turning the spare key between his fingers. Each knew his or her moment: Walter would raise the missing train, Meera the hidden fees and Fergus the red clay on the key, but only after Edith had given the signal. Gwen Hartley, who had insisted on coming, sat in the front row and promised not to say a word.

On Thursday morning the lounge at Maple Court was full to the doors, with the residents ranged in rows on the hard chairs and the staff standing along the walls. Harold Stott took his place at the front in a fresh grey suit, with his briefcase at his feet and his round face arranged in an expression of kindly regret. In the next room, behind a half-open door, Sergeant Rudd settled himself with his notebook on his knee.

Harold Stott opened the meeting by thanking everyone for coming, in the soothing tone of a man delivering a small piece of bad news, and then explained that the sale of the garden would go ahead after all. The company needed the money, he said, and nothing could be done, though he hoped the residents would understand that it was nobody's fault. A groan rolled around the room like distant thunder, and Gwen Hartley gripped her stick.

Edith rose from her chair, thanked Mr Stott with the courtesy of a headteacher at prize-giving, and asked the residents to spare a thought for Conrad Vane. She said only that he had been found in the glasshouse on Sunday morning after a fall, and that the police had very nearly decided it was a sad accident. She mentioned no details whatever, and she did not so much as glance toward the gap in the next door.

Harold Stott shook his heavy head and sighed with great feeling, saying how dreadful it was to think of poor Conrad lying there under that avalanche of broken pots, pulled down on top of him by who knew whom. He had meant it as an expression of sympathy, but the words had scarcely left his lips before he realised that he had said something very strange indeed. The silence in the room became absolute, and in the next room Sergeant Rudd stopped writing.

How strange, Edith remarked gently, that Mr Stott should know that the pots had been pulled down on top of the poor man, since no one outside the police station had been told it. She had been given that fact in confidence by the sergeant himself, she said, and she had repeated it only to three friends, none of whom had spoken a word of it to the staff. The room, which had been quiet before, now seemed to hold its breath and wait for whatever would come next.

Harold Stott swung round, his rosy face suddenly pale, and blustered that Joe must have told him, or one of the kitchen staff, or perhaps some helpful person whose name he could not recall. From the back of the lounge Joe Bell unfolded his arms and said slowly that he had spoken to the sergeant and to nobody else, and would swear to it on any book Mr Stott liked. Heads turned from one man to the other like spectators at a tennis match, and nobody breathed.

Now Walter Pike rose to his full height and held up the yellow railway notice like a banner, announcing that no trains had run on Saturday and that the quarter-past-six to London had existed only in Mr Stott's imagination. Meera followed him, reading aloud from a pile of statements that fourteen residents had been paying a mysterious administration fee for two years. Murmurs of anger rose from the rows of chairs, and Harold Stott took a step backward.

Fergus Lyle stood last and lifted the spare glasshouse key high, so that everyone could see the brick-red stain on its paper tag and along its worn teeth. Only three people knew the code to the cabinet, he said, and one of them was Mr Stott, whose shoes had carried the very same clay on Monday morning. He laid the key quietly on the table between them, like a card at the end of a game.

Harold Stott's round face crumpled, and he sank heavily into a chair with his head in his hands while the whole lounge watched in horrified silence. In a broken voice he confessed that he had been taking the residents' money for years, and that Conrad Vane had found out and summoned him to the glasshouse to say that he would tell the police. Then, in a moment of panic, he had struck him with a clay pot, locked the door and invented a story about a train that he had known from the beginning could never hold.

The door of the next room swung fully open, and Sergeant Tom Rudd stepped through it with his notebook in one hand and a pair of handcuffs, which he had hoped not to need, in the other. In a quiet, formal voice he arrested Harold Stott for the death of Conrad Vane and for the theft of the residents' money, and Stott, shrunken and grey, allowed himself to be led away without another word. For a long moment, nobody in the lounge moved, and then somebody began, very quietly, to clap.

In the weeks that followed, careful police accountants traced the stolen money through a maze of Stott's private bank accounts and recovered nearly all of it. A lawyer appointed by the court arranged for every resident to be repaid in full, and Gwen Hartley, who had been the first to show her statement to Meera, was invited to receive her cheque first. She folded it into her handbag with a satisfied nod, remarking that it was about time.

Mr Vane's only relative, his sister Ruth, inherited Maple Court and travelled down to Willowby to put his affairs in order, and Edith handed her the letter from the seed tin with a sense of ceremony. Ruth read it twice, wiped her eyes, and then signed a legal paper declaring that the garden would never be sold, which was exactly what her brother had decided on the final day of his life. It seemed to everyone that he had been rather a better man than they had thought.

Joe Bell kept his job and his vegetables, and on a bright, cool morning in autumn the whole house gathered beside the rose walk to watch Gwen Hartley plant one more bush. It was a deep white rose, chosen in memory of Conrad Vane, and she patted down the earth around it with a small, gloved hand while Joe leaned on his spade and pretended not to be moved. Nobody spoke for a while, because there seemed to be nothing left to say.

On the following Wednesday, at exactly three o'clock, Sergeant Rudd appeared at the door of the Garden Room carrying a box of iced buns in one hand and a thick cardboard folder in the other. The police, he said a little shyly, could occasionally use advice from people with sharper eyes than their own, and he wondered whether the Wednesday Club might consider an unofficial puzzle. The four friends exchanged glances in which delight and dignity struggled for the upper hand.

In the long gold light of the evening the four friends carried their tea out into the garden and sat among the roses with the glasshouse glowing behind them like a lantern. The trouble was over, the thief was caught, and the garden would belong to Maple Court for as long as anyone could imagine, and the folder of cuttings lay unopened on Edith's knee. Edith smiled at her three friends and said that there was no hurry, because the best puzzles, like the best cakes, were meant to be shared.
